Q: Is switching from C++ to Python for DSA a good decision? A:

What do you intend to do? What are your long term goals? You can have a long and enriching career in programming and not know either of those languages. A gentleman I work with was almost 100% Pascal and Delphi. Occasionally he'd pull out the C for a job, but he wasn't very good at it. I don't think he wrote a line of C++ or Python. Which is cool. My Pascal is probably trash. My C++ struggled for a few years as it slowly sunk in that the best way to write C++ code was not throw C and Java into a blender and hit the puree button. The best way was to sit down with a couple good books and actually <expletive deleted>ing learn C++. I wish I'd paid more attention to Haskell; it can really change the way you think about composing a program. And that's what you want, really, different ways to approach writing programs, even if you steal a trick from LISP and use it in C when it makes sense to do it.

You're probably not going to make a living off the prizes in DSA competitions. Don't totally ignore the stuff, the more tools you have in your box the better. It's also known to make it easier to get past the HR firewall at some companies, especially as a junior. Algorithms and data structures is mostly language agnostic. Over my too-long stay in post-secondary education, I took DSA courses in Pascal, Modula, C, and Java. Every time I went back to school, new mandatory Datastructures class in a new language. The course was pretty much the exact same every time. This is also partly due to course lesson plans being reused and adapted as languages come in and go out of style. I was chuckling over the echoes of Pascal and C thinking in a Java course because the course had been adapted from Pascal to C and then Java. When I pointed it out to my boss, he read over some of the material and pointed to hints of Fortran beneath what I'd noticed.

It seems that this applies to stacks even more than individual languages. I don't work in that field, but I've still been exposed to MEAN, MERN, and at least three different spins on LAMP. Next year could be the year of FROOtBAT. It's always changing, so make sure you learn the ideologies and idioms stacks are implementing so that you can quickly pick up the next hip stack.

We're not so much in the business of writing code as we are in solving problems. Once we figure out what the problem really is and break it down into little problems, we reach into our toolbox and see what tool best solves each of those little problems. And sometimes you take the second-or-third best tool because it integrates better with the rest of the system. The bigger your tool box, the more choice you have and the more likely .

Q: Can you dereference a pointer to a destroyed object? A:

There are a handful of special cases where this is allowed, to refer to a different object created in the same storage as the destroyed object. To quote the Standard, at [pointer.launder] (emphasis added):

If a new object is created in storage occupied by an existing object of the same type, a pointer to the original object can be used to refer to the new object unless its complete object is a const object or it is a base class subobject; in the latter cases, this function [std::launder] can be used to obtain a usable pointer to the new object.

There is language elsewhere restricting this to situations where the destroyed object is “transparently replaceable” with the new one, which can get complicated. But a new object of a type that is compatible with the original pointer does transparently replace the old one, unless the old one was a base class or a const object.

By the way, if you search for std::launder, you will find that a small handful of prolific posters have been very active in spreading the idea that C++ programs need to std::launder practically every reinterpret_cast. This is incorrect. if you read what std::launder actually does, it’s only used in a small number of special cases where the compiler would otherwise be allowed to assume that the a location contains the same object as before, but it has in fact been replaced.

Q: How and where mnemonic/private keys are generated/stored in IOS for mobile non-custodial wallet A:

No, that's not necessarily correct.

Q1: A private key or seed generated outside the Secure Enclave can still be protected using the Secure Enclave. A common approach is to encrypt the mnemonic/seed with a key stored in the Secure Enclave (or Android Keystore/StrongBox) and save the encrypted data in app storage. The seed itself does not have to be generated inside the enclave.

Q2: In most non-custodial wallets:

  • The mnemonic is generated by the wallet using a cryptographically secure random number generator.

  • The seed/private keys are derived from the mnemonic (BIP-39/BIP-32).

  • The mnemonic or seed is stored encrypted in app storage.

  • The encryption key is protected by the Secure Enclave/Keystore and may be gated by biometrics or a PIN.

The Secure Enclave's main role is usually to protect encryption keys and sensitive cryptographic operations, not to replace the mnemonic based recovery mechanism. Since users must be able to back up and restore their wallets, the mnemonic must remain exportable and cannot be permanently locked inside the enclave.
